headline: Market price is a function of objective earnings and subjective sentiment; value investors can predict the former but not the latter, and that asymmetry is their edge
reasoning: Howard Coleman articulates a core value investing principle: share price is determined by two components — an objective factor (earnings) and a subjective factor (market sentiment, i.e. how optimistic or pessimistic participants are about those future earnings). He argues that no investor can reliably predict sentiment, but value investors can get better and better at predicting earnings. When earnings are predictable and trending upward, sentiment volatility becomes an opportunity rather than a threat. He uses the analogy of playing poker against drunk opponents — if you understand the fundamentals, you can exploit their irrational bets.
quote: By definition, the price of an asset? In this case, a share price is made up of an objective and a subjective factor. That objective factor is its earnings, and the subjective factor is how euphoric or pessimistic are people in the market participating in an auction about the future of those earnings? So as a value investor, you can never predict the likely optimism or pessimism... But what you can do is get better and better at predicting the earnings. And in the long run, given that that sentiment will move, we talk about as a sine curve. It goes up and down, optimism to pessimism and then back. If the earnings are going up predictably and you're good at predicting those earnings, then the second half of that equation is your friend, not your enemy.

headline: Peter Rogers sells ANZ — earnings flat for 10 years, falling margins, dividend yield equals risk-free rate, banks still expensive versus global peers

headline: Named alongside CSL as a higher-quality turnaround story preferable to investing in Lendlease's strategic reset

headline: Sold — no stable earnings, capital-intensive mining model with a decades-long project pipeline

headline: Team Invest's Andrew Coleman is uninterested in Argo Investments LIC, arguing the 16-17% NTA discount is insufficient to justify paying for external fund management

headline: Andrew Coleman rates JB Hi-Fi a buy at 17x PE, calling it one of the world's top handful of retailers by sales per square foot

headline: PE of ~100x means gravity will reassert itself; rated hold or sell despite strong business fundamentals
reasoning: Coleman acknowledges Pro Medicus is a wonderful company growing 25-30% p.a. with high return on equity (~40%) and strong stability. headline: Andrew Coleman rates Tyro a sell, seeing no moat in a crowded payments market and a PE of 19x offering insufficient compensation for regulatory risk
reasoning: Coleman is uncertain whether Tyro has any meaningful moats in a space with hundreds of global competitors. headline: Andrew Coleman rates Baby Bunting a sell — profit flat over 10 years, high debt, and once traded at 100x PE making it still overvalued at current levels

headline: Andrew Coleman avoids Southern Cross Electrical despite strong fundamentals, arguing it lacks durable moats beyond the current data centre rollout cycle
reasoning: Coleman acknowledges Southern Cross has all the basic hallmarks of a quality long-term investment — profitable, growing earnings at double digits, high stability, little or no debt. However, his 700-member investment community concluded it lacks durable moats; it is simply benefiting from the rising tide of data centre rollout where all providers can currently charge outsized margins. When that tide turns, the question is whether the business has something to protect it — Coleman and his members see no compelling answer and therefore avoid.
quote: It's actually a company we spent a bit of time on with our membership over the last sort of 12 to 18 months, right? Because, you know, the numbers starting to look really good. The growth is clearly there. The stability actually has been over the last few years as well. There's little or no debt. So, it's got all those fundamental basic requirements of being a wonderful long-term investment. The bit that it doesn't have, at least in our 700 members view, and I would agree with them, is it doesn't have the moats. It's benefiting right now simply because the rising tide is lifting all boats in the providers to these data centers. You know, the data center rollout is happening. It's happening quick. The price to get the things inside, whether that's the GPUs, the wiring, the cabling, the racks, they are all going through the roof and the providers of those picks and shovels have a unique current position where they're able to charge an outsized margin. The problem is going to be at some point that tide will turn and when it does, the question will be, are they swimming naked or does this business have something to protect it? And unfortunately, for any holder of Southern Cross Electrical, I don't see those moats and neither do our members.

headline: Andrew Coleman says take profits on SRG Global at 36.5x PE as cyclical peak approaches, and warns against fresh capital at these levels

headline: Andrew Coleman rates Amotiv a sell and prefers ARB which offers double the ROE and growth rate for the same PE
